headlines.title: GM aims to develop vehicles in as little as two years with AI, software push
headlines.summary: General Motors is targeting a roughly two-year vehicle development cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software.
headlines.article_text: GM aims to shorten vehicle development time with AI, software push Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points General Motors is hoping to reduce the time it takes to develop vehicles, targeting a roughly two-year cycle as it expands its use of artificial intelligence, simulation and vehicle software. GM says it is using artificial intelligence, simulation and more concurrent engineering to shorten development and reduce physical testing. The automaker is also expanding in-vehicle AI and plans to introduce eyes-off highway driving beginning with the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. In this article GM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:20 04:20 Highlights from GM Forward 2026 Power Lunch NEW YORK — General Motors plans to lean into artificial intelligence and vehicle software for future growth and development amid increasing competition abroad from Chinese automakers and a tougher U.S. market. The Detroit automaker on Wednesday shared new details about a proprietary AI agent it's releasing under its OnStar brand, plans for a fourth generation of more efficient all-electric vehicles and a target to cut its vehicle development time in half. GM also reconfirmed that by 2028 , it wants to have eyes-off highway driving, or "personal autonomy," that will let drivers take their attention off the road. The automaker said that technology would start with the Cadillac Escalade IQ EV before rolling out to other, more high-volume models. "All of these developments are building us the car of the future," CEO Mary Barra said Wednesday during an event laying out the plans, called "GM Forward," in downtown Manhattan. The initiatives, which Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and other executives discussed at the event, are designed to streamline the automaker's operations, while also improving the capabilities of its vehicles for customers. "Over the last 12 months, we've evolved how we design, engineer and build our vehicles," said Anderson, who led the event and who has been tasked with overseeing GM's latest technology transformation. Read more CNBC auto news Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity How lower fuel economy targets could boost pickups and V-8 engines Stellantis CEO urges incentives for carmakers who build in Europe as Chinese rivals gain ground GM said it is now targeting a vehicle development time of roughly two years from concept to production versus a traditional four- to five-year cycle. However, the company did not detail a timeline for reaching that goal. The event comes as Chinese automakers are growing outside of the U.S. with rapid development times of new technologies and vehicles. Consulting firm AlixPartners said it believes China is currently bringing vehicles to market twice as fast as traditional automakers, with 40% to 50% less investment and a 30% cost advantage. GM also continues to play catch-up to U.S. EV leader Tesla when it comes to delivering technology advancements through over-the-air updates and automated driving capabilities . Anderson, a former Tesla executive, declined to speak specifically about how GM's technologies will compare to the EV maker, but said GM's systems will be able to visualize, or see, more things through the use of multiple types of sensors than a strictly camera-based system, which Tesla uses. He also said the rapid development and new software architecture will help the company better compete against Chinese automakers abroad. "There's inherent virtue to speed," Anderson told CNBC during an interview after the event. "Not just in being able to get a car out faster, it's being able to develop a system that's far more performant that you could have otherwise." Next-generation vehicles GM said Wednesday it has major plans for its next generation of EVs and traditional vehicles with internal combustion engines. The company said those coming vehicles — regardless of type — will have 40 times the computing power and up to 50% faster cellular connectivity than prior systems. That computing power is expected to help the automaker with over-the-air updates, onboard diagnostics and AI, as well as other technologies such as automated driving features. The new brain of the vehicle will launch on the $130,000 Cadillac Escalade IQ EV in 2028 before rolling out to other models, including its next generation of EVs. CEO and Chair of General Motors Mary Barra delivers a speech during the brand's annual technology event in New York on Oct. 21, 2026. Charly Triballeau | AFP | Getty Images GM said the forthcoming EVs are expected to be 25% more aerodynamic and 15% lighter and feature electric motors and battery packs that are more compact. GM President Mark Reuss said despite lackluster consumer adoption and the automaker pulling back billions of dollars in investments in EVs , it remains committed to producing them. "We continue to develop our future EVs and work to reduce battery costs," Reuss said during the event. "And when the U.S. market is ready for EVs in large numbers, we will be there for them." AI development GM expects to achieve such targets through the use of AI in research and development. The company said it is developing a "new operating approach for vehicle development" that leans into enterprise AI and virtualization to increase speed. "This concurrent engineering model allows us to innovate faster, improve continuously, and scale new technologies across our lineup with incredible agility," the company said in a release. From left, GM CEO Mary Barra, Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson and President Mark Reuss at the company's GM Forward event in downtown Manhattan on Oct. 21, 2026. Michael Wayland | CNBC GM used the development of its next-generation vehicles, including a new battery chemistry, as an example of how the new technologies are reshaping its vehicle development. The company said it virtually tested more than 300,000 battery designs using its recently announced lithium manganese rich battery chemistry, or LMR, before building a single physical prototype. Anderson said Wednesday that LMR will be the exclusive battery tech for its fourth-generation EVs. GM had previously said it wanted to use those batteries in full-size electric vehicles such as its Chevrolet Silverado and Escalade IQ beginning in 2028. Anderson said GM is uniquely positioned to use AI compared to other automotive companies because of its more than 100 years in the industry as well as 30 years of OnStar. "In the age of AI, data is currency," Anderson said. "For decades, GM's engineering, manufacturing and product teams have generated unparalleled body of data that we're now using to build industry-leading AI tools." In-vehicle AI The company is building on its internal use of AI to better shape its experiences for customers. GM on Wednesday reconfirmed that it plans to launch a proprietary in-vehicle AI assistant through its OnStar technology brand. Here's how it did compared to LSEG estimates: Earnings per share : $3.83 Revenue : $64.60 billion vs $63.37 billion It was not immediately clear if earnings were comparable to the $5.75 per share expected by analysts. Revenue jumped 26% from a year ago. "We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone - including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model," said CEO Mark Zuckerberg in the earnings release. The initial success of the Muse AI personal assistant tool that debuted in September shot to the top of Apple's iOS app store. That AI momentum helped Meta end September with its best month on Wall Street since 2022. Meta isn't the first to create a digital assistant that can organize people's email and scan the web for headphone deals, but the company's empire, which includes Facebook and Instagram, has helped introduce AI agents to the masses. At the same time, Meta and its AI chief Alexandr Wang have continued rolling out new foundation models and related updates at a speedy clip, including Muse Wonder , which was released last Monday. Wall Street is monitoring Meta's capex spending as the company further develops the underlying computing infrastructure needed to power AI agents and foundation models. — Jonathan Vanian 14 Min Ago Meta misses on third-quarter daily active people Meta's third-quarter daily active people, or DAP, came in at 3.64 billion, trailing the 3.65 billion that analysts were expecting, according to StreetAccount. That figure represents all of Meta's users across its family of apps like Facebook and Instagram. — Jonathan Vanian 16 Min Ago Meta posts fourth-quarter sales guidance Meta said that it expects fourth-quarter revenue guidance to come between $73 billion to $76 billion. That range's midpoint is above analyst estimates of $73.73 billion. — Jonathan Vanian 29 Min Ago What's Meta to do with all this compute? Alexandr Wang, chief AI officer of Meta, during the Bloomberg Tech conference in San Francisco, California, US, on Thursday, June 4, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Since Zuckerberg spent billions of dollars overhauling the company's AI unit and placed Wang as the division's leader some 14 months ago, analysts at Baird Equity Research have noticed increased "positive sentiment" from investors, according to a Tuesday note that cited optimism over the Muse AI agents and related technologies. The Baird analysts said that while Meta's AI investments will help with future AI agent and foundation model monetization efforts, they "will continue to be the bigger needle-mover to quarterly results in the near-term." That's because those AI investments will still be improving Meta's underlying online advertising platform that companies use to send targeted advertisements, they explained. Investors have questioned why Meta needs to spend that much money on data centers when it doesn't have a cloud computing business like rivals Google and Amazon. Wall Street may be more willing to cut the social network some slack because of its recent AI momentum. The Baird analysts wrote: As such, our ad checks are generally positive for Meta, and we expect an in-line Q3 report; we believe the street is better-informed on capex/margin pressures, and we believe a scenario where Meta raises capex guidance (2026/2027) could be received more positively (or less negatively) by investors now that the company is demonstrating a clearer ROI, despite the lack of a cloud platform. — Jonathan Vanian 35 Min Ago How Meta could make money from Muse Cheng Xin | Getty Images Meta is offering $20 and $100 monthly subscription plans for Muse AI agent power users. The company is also charging developers $50 or $200 a month to access its most powerful Muse Wonder Full AI model via the Muse coding agent that debuted in early August. Meta's nascent subscription efforts represent opportunities for the company to expand beyond online advertising , which is still its core money maker. Investors have been concerned about the Facebook parent's hefty AI investments relative to rivals like Alphabet and Amazon that have cloud computing businesses . While AI-specific monetization efforts offer hope of diversification, they remains a longer-term play. Last week, Meta teamed up with longtime rival Apple to make Meta's new open-weight AI model work with the iPhone maker's high-end Mac computers. Unlike Meta's proprietary AI models, coders can download the weights of Muse Spark Open for free . Meta is betting that developers who try Muse Spark Open may eventually want to pay to access the company's more powerful proprietary AI systems. "These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said in an interview with CNBC. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage." — Jonathan Vanian 40 Min Ago Meta Reality Labs expected to continue bleeding money Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive officer of Meta Platforms Inc., left, and Andrew Bosworth, chief technology officer and head of Reality Labs, wear Meta Ray-Ban Display AI glasses during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 17, 2025. headlines.article_text: Meta ordered to pay $25B in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal in New Mexico. The penalty comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data. A New Mexico district court judge said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg attends the annual Allen and Co. Sun Valley Media and Technology Conference at the Sun Valley Resort in Sun Valley, Idaho, U.S., July 9, 2026. Brendan McDermid | Reuters Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago. The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services. Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion. "The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing. The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full. "For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences." Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal." "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online." Read more CNBC tech news Meta earnings updates: AI spending, ad revenue and stock reaction Tesla earnings loom after Musk calls SpaceX merger a 'good idea' Intel hits construction milestone at Ohio chip fab that's at least 5 years behind schedule Investors are questioning neoclouds' business model but Nebius says AI computing prices are rising Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September. In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices. Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations. "Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial. Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance. Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds
headlines.summary: Rick Rieder, BlackRock's CIO of global fixed income, lays out his expectations for the fourth quarter and where he sees the best opportunities.
headlines.article_text: Rick Rieder sees historic opportunity in investment-grade bonds Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points BlackRock's Rick Rieder is bullish on this area of the credit market for the first time in a "long time." The CIO of global fixed income lays out his fourth-quarter fixed-income outlook in an exclusive interview. In this article BLK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Rick Rieder speaking at the CNBC CEO Council Summit in Washington, D.C. on June 2, 2026. Aaron Clamage | CNBC Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview. Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration. "Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook , released Wednesday. That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance." While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus. The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC) , which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit. iShares Flexible Income Active ETF year to date Best opportunities include hyperscalers Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3. That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG. "They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it." Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July , that stood at 8.5%. That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised. "Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield." Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names. "There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be." The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out. Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle , which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits. CoreWeave's 2031 bond yield on Oct. 21, 2026 Fed watch Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve , which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool . The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said. "They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure." Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added. Calculating risks ahead Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026. "The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said. Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched. "With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on." In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said. headlines.article_text: Musk's Trump Account SpaceX stock is 'tip of the iceberg': Gerstner Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points In an X post on Monday, Elon Musk said that he will give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year. Brad Gerstner, founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, said on Wednesday that the gift would go to Trump Accounts in an exclusive interview on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," said Gerstner. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 6:47 06:47 Brad Gerstner on Trump Accounts: One of the most successful changes to our social contract in 100 years Squawk Box Elon Musk said earlier this week that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX next year, and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner said Wednesday that the stock donations would come via Trump Accounts . If it happens, that donation of $10.5 billion worth of shares is just the beginning, according to Gerstner, the founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, the new tax-deferred investing accounts for children. "Elon is the tip of the iceberg," Gerstner told CNBC's "Squawk Box" in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. "This is the most giving country on the planet," he said. "I told the president, I think I can raise $100 billion over the course of the next 12 months to sponsor all of the kids in America." In addition to Musk, Gerstner said he had also talked to "every major tech CEO and founder." A $100 billion fundraising target would represent about one-sixth of all U.S. charitable giving. Americans donated $592.5 billion in 2024, according to the latest data from the National Philanthropic Trust . Gerstner has committed about $35 million to help seed the investment accounts for kids in his home state of Indiana. Read more CNBC personal finance coverage CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September, which allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds . "The Treasury targeted this carve-out at mega-donors and large philanthropic foundations, such as the Dells, who made a multibillion-dollar charitable pledge," said Adam Bergman, founder of IRA Financial and a tax attorney based in Miami. "It allows them to donate large blocks of publicly traded stock without triggering substantial capital-gains taxes." The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale gifts, and a number of other philanthropists are poised to participate, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano also told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Oct. 8. "They range from small to mega," he said. "We do have mega donors in the nine-digit range, you know, bunches of them." In the broader world of charitable giving, Treasury's temporary regulations also give donors unusual influence over children's investments , according to lawyers and philanthropic experts who spoke with CNBC. Future Trump Account expansion "As @TrumpAccounts continues to grow we look forward to more philanthropists joining the movement and helping children across America jumpstart their financial future," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an X post Monday . The latest Trump Account comments come weeks after the Treasury Department auto-enrolled more than 60 million children . Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts , are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number. Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also claim a one-time $ 1,000 pilot program contribution from the Treasury. Gerstner also said Wednesday that there is a push to expand access to the accounts to all U.S. citizens under age 40. "Why not pull forward 20 years of IRAs? We can create all of those today," he said. "So if Elon says then, I want to give to everyone under 40, or OpenAI says I want to give to everyone under 40, there's a vehicle, there's a vessel that they can start compounding in ... those are the types of things we are working on." In addition to more than 70 million children under 18 in the U.S., about 90 million U.S. citizens are between 18 and 40 years of age, according to CNBC's analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data. However, expanding Trump Accounts to Americans under age 40 would require a legislative change from Congress. In an X post on Tuesday , Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, called the proposed expansion a "game-changer," and said he would "lead the bill in the Senate to make it happen." Gerstner told CNBC on Wednesday that expanding the Trump Account age limit is "wildly popular" among congressional Democrats and Republicans. But it's unclear whether the proposal has the legislative backing needed to become law.
